title: 2 Samuel 22:1–16
context: David’s song of deliverance, closely paralleling Psalm 18 with some differences in wording. The opening stanza praises the LORD as rock and deliverer and describes, in storm imagery, God coming down in answer to David’s cry.

verses.text: David spoke to the LORD the words of this song in the day that the LORD delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul,
verses.arminianNotes: David sings “in the day that the LORD delivered him out of the hand of all his enemies, and out of the hand of Saul.” Arminian readers see praise flowing from real experiences of rescue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God credited with every deliverance. The song closely parallels Psalm 18, with wording differences between the two that this note does not try to harmonize.

verses.text: and he said: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer, even mine;
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.” Arminian readers see personal trust in God expressed through images of strength and safety, offered freely by a grateful servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithfulness confessed in vivid images. The theme of the LORD as deliverer is shared ground for readers in both traditions throughout this song.

verses.text: God is my rock in whom I take refuge; my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower, and my refuge. My savior, you save me from violence.
verses.arminianNotes: “God is my rock in whom I take refuge … My savior, you save me from violence.” Arminian readers see a believer choosing to rely on God rather than human defenses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God as the source of all protection. The piling up of titles expresses complete dependence on God for safety and salvation in danger.

verses.text: I call on the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; So shall I be saved from my enemies.
verses.arminianNotes: “I call on the LORD, who is worthy to be praised; So shall I be saved from my enemies.” Arminian readers see calling on God as the believer’s response that God graciously answers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see prayer and praise joined. The verse expresses confidence that God hears and saves, a pattern repeated throughout the song.

verses.text: For the waves of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: “For the waves of death surrounded me. The floods of ungodliness made me afraid.” Arminian readers see real fear in the face of mortal danger, voiced honestly by God’s servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vivid images of peril. The language of overwhelming waters conveys helplessness that only God can overcome.

verses.text: The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death caught me.
verses.arminianNotes: “The cords of Sheol were around me. The snares of death caught me.” Arminian readers see death pictured as a hunter’s trap, emphasizing how close David came to destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of death closing in. Sheol is the place of the dead; that is a translation rendering, not a textual variant.

verses.text: In my distress, I called on the LORD. Yes, I called to my God. He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry came into his ears.
verses.arminianNotes: “In my distress, I called on the LORD … He heard my voice out of his temple.” Arminian readers see God responding personally to the cry of a distressed believer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God hearing from his dwelling. The verse anchors the dramatic description that follows in an answered prayer.

verses.text: Then the earth shook and trembled. The foundations of heaven quaked and were shaken, because he was angry.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then the earth shook and trembled … because he was angry.” Arminian readers see poetic imagery portraying God’s powerful intervention on behalf of his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a theophany describing God’s mighty coming. Readers in this tradition generally read the cosmic imagery as poetic expression of real divine action.

verses.text: Smoke went up out of his nostrils. Consuming fire came out of his mouth. Coals were kindled by it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Smoke went up out of his nostrils. Consuming fire came out of his mouth.” Arminian readers see vivid imagery of God’s righteous anger against those who threatened his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see figurative language for God’s holy power. The imagery recalls other appearances of God in fire and smoke in Israel’s story.

verses.text: He bowed the heavens also, and came down. Thick darkness was under his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: “He bowed the heavens also, and came down. Thick darkness was under his feet.” Arminian readers see God personally entering the struggle to rescue his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s condescension to save. The image of God coming down expresses his active involvement in the deliverance of his people.

verses.text: He rode on a cherub, and flew. Yes, he was seen on the wings of the wind.
verses.arminianNotes: “He rode on a cherub, and flew. Yes, he was seen on the wings of the wind.” Arminian readers see poetic imagery stressing the speed and power of God’s help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see figurative language for God’s sovereign rule over creation. The cherub imagery connects with the ark and God’s throne in Israel’s worship.

verses.text: He made darkness a shelter around himself, gathering of waters, and thick clouds of the skies.
verses.arminianNotes: “He made darkness a shelter around himself, gathering of waters, and thick clouds of the skies.” Arminian readers see God’s majesty veiled even as he acts to save.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s hiddenness and glory together. The storm imagery portrays a God who is both near to help and beyond human sight.

verses.text: At the brightness before him, coals of fire were kindled.
verses.arminianNotes: “At the brightness before him, coals of fire were kindled.” Arminian readers see the overwhelming radiance of God’s presence as he comes to deliver his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see brightness amid darkness as a picture of God’s glory. The imagery highlights the holiness of the God who rescues.

verses.text: The LORD thundered from heaven. The Most High uttered his voice.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD thundered from heaven. The Most High uttered his voice.” Arminian readers see thunder as poetic expression of God’s powerful response to prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s voice as sovereign and decisive. The title “Most High” stresses his supremacy over every enemy.

verses.text: He sent out arrows and scattered them, lightning and confused them.
verses.arminianNotes: “He sent out arrows and scattered them, lightning and confused them.” Arminian readers see God fighting for his servant against those who opposed him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God as the divine warrior. The arrows and lightning portray God’s decisive action against enemies who could not withstand him.

verses.text: Then the channels of the sea appeared. The foundations of the world were laid bare by the LORD’s rebuke, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
verses.arminianNotes: “The foundations of the world were laid bare by the LORD’s rebuke.” Arminian readers see God’s power over creation employed to rescue his servant from danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see creation itself responding to God’s word. The imagery recalls God’s power over the waters, a theme found elsewhere in Israel’s worship.
